```{r}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "../cases/eu-frames")
```

```{r}
#| label: page-numbers
#| include: false
# The numbers quoted in section 5, computed from the curve of the case; the
# code shown in sections 4 and 5 does not run.
eu_curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
eu_ref   <- eu_curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
num <- \(x, d = 3) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about R, the language in which the analysis of the course is written, as the EU-frames case uses it. The first steps in R, from objects and data frames to the pipe, the datawizard verbs, a first table and a first figure, are taught in the module of the same name on the housing-audit site, [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/companion/intro-r.html), which assumes no programming at all and works on a file small enough to look at whole, with an outcome that is either yes or no. This page assumes those steps. After a short description of R, the IDE and the three surfaces into which R is typed, it takes the tools to the country-year panel of the EU-frames case, a table of 270 rows built from Eurobarometer surveys: the formats in which data arrive and the packages that fetch them, the grammar of graphics in depth, and the specification curve of the case.

The panel is the material for two things that a file of yes-or-no outcomes cannot show. A scatterplot with a fitted line needs measures that vary continuously, and the panel holds them, among them the unemployment rate and the mean score with which the respondents of a country-year framed the EU in cosmopolitan terms. The curve of the case mixes predictors whose results point in opposite directions, so it has to be aligned with the claim before it can be read.

The code of sections 4 and 5 is shown without being run, because it reads the panel of the case, which is on your machine once you have the workspace, and the numbers quoted in section 5 are computed from the curve of the case when the page is built. The way to learn is still to type. Copy each block into the workspace that you downloaded from the [setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html#the-workspace) and run it there.

The courses use the module at several points. It is the companion of the R tutorial in Part 2 of the [one-day course on data tools](../tracks/eu-frames-one-day-data-tools/part-2.qmd) and of the first session of [day 2](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/day-2.qmd) of the three-day course.

## 1. R and the IDE {#sec-what}

**R** is a programming language built for working with data: reading it, reshaping it, fitting statistical models to it and drawing figures from it. It is free and open source, and it is one of the common languages of quantitative social science, which is why the analysis of the course is written in it. On its own, R is a program that reads instructions and returns answers.

**The IDE** is the program from which you drive R. An IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), short for integrated development environment, is a window with your files on one side, a place to write and run code, and panels that show results, figures and the objects you have made. Newcomers often run the language and the environment together, although each is installed separately. You install R once, so that the language is on your machine, and you install an IDE once, as the place where you work. When the IDE first opens, it finds the R that you installed and connects to it. The [setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html) walks through both installations, and the [IDE module](ide.qmd) sets the three common IDEs side by side, pane by pane.

## 2. The console, the script and the report {#sec-surfaces}

There are three surfaces into which you type R, and knowing which is for what saves a great deal of confusion later.

The **console** is the interactive prompt. You type one line, press Enter, and R answers immediately. It is the place to try something out, check a value or do a quick sum. Its weakness is that everything typed there is lost when the session closes, with no record of how you reached a result.

A **script** is a plain text file with the extension `.R` that holds a sequence of commands you want to keep. You write the commands in the script and send them to the console from there, all at once or line by line. A script runs the same way tomorrow and on someone else's machine, and it shows step by step how a result was produced. The course follows a simple rule: try things in the console, and move anything that matters into a script.

A **Quarto document**, with the extension `.qmd`, is a script and a written report in one file. It holds ordinary prose with blocks of R code, called chunks, between the paragraphs. When the document is rendered, R runs every chunk and places its results, whether tables, figures or numbers, into the finished report at the point where they belong. The workspace of the course holds the same exercise in both forms: `working_script.R` takes you through Tasks 1 to 5 as a plain script, and `index.qmd` is the report that you fill in and render. The [Quarto module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/companion/quarto.html) of the housing-audit site shows how such a document is written.

## 3. Other formats, and fetching data {#sec-formats}

Survey archives distribute their files in the formats of Stata (`.dta`) and SPSS (`.sav`), and R reads both through the haven package, one function for each format, `haven::read_dta()` and `haven::read_sav()`. These formats differ from a CSV in storing **labelled data**. Each column can carry a variable label, a short description of what it holds, and a column of numeric codes can carry value labels, the words for which the codes stand. haven keeps both. `as_label()` from the sjlabelled package turns the codes into their labels, which gives a factor, and leaves out the labels of codes that no row holds, which `as_factor()` from haven would keep as empty levels. Labels are metadata that somebody typed, and they can be wrong, so read them as a first guide and the codebook as the authority. The Eurobarometer waves of the EU-frames case arrive from the GESIS archive as Stata files, with value labels on their answer codes, and the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-build) builds the respondent file from them.

Many organisations keep their data in **Excel** files, and the `readxl` package reads them one sheet at a time, since a workbook is really a stack of tables. The file names in this block and the next are illustrative, since the course ships no workbook and no Parquet file:

```r
rates <- readxl::read_excel("unemployment_rates.xlsx", sheet = "annual")
```

Treat what arrives from a spreadsheet with mild suspicion. Excel displays one thing and stores another often enough – dates especially – that column types should be checked with `summary()` straight after every import.

Finally, **Parquet** and **Feather** are the newer columnar formats, which store a table column by column, and you will increasingly meet them where datasets are large or move between programming languages. They are compressed and fast, and unlike a CSV they store the type of each column inside the file, so nothing has to be re-inferred on reading. The `arrow` package reads both, and the small `nanoparquet` package reads and writes Parquet without needing any other package:

```r
panel <- arrow::read_parquet("EUframes_cy.parquet")   # arrow::read_feather() for Feather
```

Whatever the source format, what you end up with in R is the same data frame, and everything downstream – the data verbs, the models fitted in later modules – proceeds identically. Every `read_` function here also has a `write_` counterpart (`write_csv()`, `write_dta()`, `write_parquet()`, and `write_xlsx()` from the `writexl` package), so R also serves as the converter between all of these formats. The course ships its data as CSV all the same, because for tables of a few hundred or a thousand rows the efficiency of the binary formats buys nothing, while plain text can be opened in anything, compared line by line or read in an email.

### Fetching data from a repository or an API {#sec-fetching}

Most data come from an archive, a statistical office or a repository, and for many of those sources an R package fetches the data straight into a data frame. The query is then written down in your script instead of being clicked through on a website, and that is what makes the download repeatable. The [data sources module](data-sources.qmd) maps the sources and works through the routes of the case step by step, while this subsection covers the packages that query them, which fall into three groups.

**Repositories of deposited work**, which need no account for a public file. The `dataverse` package downloads a file from any Dataverse installation by the DOI of its record. `osfr` reads and writes the Open Science Framework through its API, which is how the script `R/get_data.R` in the workspace of the EU-frames case fetches its panel, and `zen4R` does the same for Zenodo, and deposits there as well. For a source with no package, `httr2` sends the request and `jsonlite` parses the answer, and `rvest` reads a table out of a web page, with the caution that scraping a site is subject to its terms and to the courtesy of not hammering it.

**Indicators from the international organisations and statistical offices**, which are open and need no account. The `WDI` package (and `wbstats`, which covers more of the World Bank databases) queries the World Bank indicators by their codes, which is how the macro variables of the EU-frames panel were obtained, as [section 3.2](data-sources.qmd#sec-worldbank) of the data sources module sets out:

```r
macro <- WDI::WDI(country = c("DE", "FR", "GB"),
                  indicator = c(unemp = "SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS", growth = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"),
                  start = 2004, end = 2013)
```

The `eurostat` package does the same for the Eurostat tables (`get_eurostat("une_rt_a")` fetches the annual unemployment table, with `restatapi` as an alternative that uses the newer API, the interface through which programs request data from Eurostat); `OECD` and the general-purpose `rsdmx` query the OECD and any other service that publishes in SDMX, the standard format in which many statistical agencies exchange data; `Rilostat` reaches ILOSTAT; `onsr` the Office for National Statistics; `wid` the World Inequality Database. Each returns a long, tidy table, one row per country and period, that pivots into whatever shape a model needs.

**Survey and census microdata behind a registration.** Packages are fewer here, and less dependable, because an archive that asks for an account and a statement of purpose seldom offers programs a way in. Where one does, the credentials belong in an environment variable or a keyring, never in the script. `ipumsr` builds and downloads IPUMS extracts through the IPUMS API and reads them with their labels. The GESIS archive, which distributes the Eurobarometer waves behind the EU-frames case, offers no such interface. The `gesisdata` package scripts the clicks of a download by driving a web browser, but it has not been updated since July 2023, and a report of a failed download, opened on its issue tracker in February 2025, has had no answer. The course therefore downloads the waves by hand, as [section 3.1](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) of the same module shows step by step. `rdhs` serves the Demographic and Health Surveys, `pewdata` the files of the Pew Research Center, and `manifestoR` the coded programmes of the Manifesto Project with an API key, and any such package is worth testing on one file before a project is built on it. Whatever the package, the file that arrives is usually Stata or SPSS, and haven reads it with its labels, as the first part of this section described.

Two habits keep a fetched dataset reproducible. Write the fetch as a function or a script of its own, save what it returns as a dated file, and read that file in the analysis, so that the analysis does not depend on the network being up or the source being unchanged. And record the version or the download date in the file name or the README, because the World Bank and Eurostat revise past years without renaming the series.

## 4. The grammar of graphics {#sec-grammar}

[Section 12 of the module on the housing-audit site](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/companion/intro-r.html#sec-ggplot) draws a first figure, and this section takes the grammar further on the panel of the EU-frames case, read as `euframes <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv")` in the workspace of the case. Its 270 rows are 27 countries in each of ten years, and its columns include the unemployment rate (`unemp`), the mean score of cosmopolitan framing of the EU among the respondents of each country-year (`mcosmo`, from 0 to 1) and whether an EU or IMF assistance programme was running (`bailout`), so it has the continuous measures that a scatterplot, a fitted line and a panel for each country need. **ggplot2**, a member of the tidyverse family of packages, is the one that draws [@WickhamEtAl2019WelcomeTidyverse]. Almost every chart on the pages and slides of the course is built with it, so reading ggplot2 code is how you satisfy yourself that a figure shows what its caption says it shows. The figures that you draw yourself, in the workspaces and the browser labs, and the live class chart on the multiverse page of the case, are drawn with tinyplot ([section 12 of the module on the housing-audit site](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/companion/intro-r.html#sec-tinyplot)), which is light enough to run in a browser. The other exceptions are the main chart of the [Multiverse page](../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd) of the EU-frames case, which a script of the course draws in the browser, the charts of the [decision map](../cases/eu-frames/map.qmd), which Observable Plot draws, and a few figures in the methods modules that packages with plotting functions of their own draw.

The name abbreviates 'the grammar of graphics', the idea that any chart can be described as a combination of a few standard parts, much as a grammar describes how words combine into sentences. ggplot2 therefore has no separate function for each chart type. It splits a figure into parts that recombine freely: the data, the mapping from columns to visual properties, the geometric shapes drawn, the scales that decide what those shapes look like, the panels that the plot is divided into, and last the labels and the styling. A scatterplot and a bar chart are two fillings of the same slots, and once you know the slots you can read the figures on this site, including kinds you have not met yet.

### Data, mapping and geometry

A plot needs data, a mapping, and at least one geom. Everything else has a default good enough to start with.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()
```

Three things happen there. `ggplot()` receives the data frame and declares which columns drive the picture. `aes()` is the **aesthetic mapping**, and it states that the unemployment rate governs horizontal position while the cosmopolitan-framing score governs vertical position. `geom_point()` adds a **geom**, a layer of geometric shapes, drawing one point per row – 270 points for 270 country-years. Axis ranges, tick marks, gridlines and the panel background are all inferred from the data, which is why this bare version is already a readable figure.

Layers are joined with `+`, never with the pipe `|>`. The reason is historical, since ggplot2 settled on `+` years before R had a native pipe. The practical consequence is that a long chain changes operator exactly once, at the point where it stops reshaping data and starts drawing, and typing `|>` where `+` belongs is among the commonest first-week errors in R.

### Mapping and setting

Every visual property of a layer can be given two ways, and confusing them is the next commonest error. Put a property inside `aes()` and it is **mapped**: its value is read from a column, it varies row by row, and ggplot2 adds a legend explaining the correspondence. Put the same property outside `aes()`, as an ordinary argument to the geom, and it is **set**, taking one fixed value for the whole layer, with no legend because there is nothing to explain.

```r
# MAPPED: colour comes from a column, so the points differ and a legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()

# SET: colour is a constant, identical for every point, and no legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.5)
```

`alpha` controls opacity, running from 0 for invisible to 1 for solid, and setting it below 1 is the standard remedy for a scatterplot where points pile up on one another. The constant `"#0e3b6a"` is a hex colour code, the dark blue that the course figures use.

Leaving out the `factor()` wrapped around `bailout` produces the wrong figure without any warning. `bailout` is stored as 0 and 1 in numeric form, so `colour = bailout` gives ggplot2 a number, which it treats as continuous, drawing a colour gradient and a legend running smoothly from 0.00 to 1.00. What you wanted was two categories in two colours, and `factor(bailout)` is how you say so. The same applies to `year`, which is also numeric: map it raw for a gradient across the decade, or wrap it in `factor()` for ten discrete groups.

### Layers

A figure can have as many layers as you need, each with its own geom, and they are drawn in the order written, so later layers cover earlier ones.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15)
```

The grey points are drawn first and the trend line over them. `geom_smooth()` fits a line through the cloud and draws it with a band showing the uncertainty around it, and `method = "lm"` asks for a straight line from the same least-squares method that the statistical methods module uses to fit models. R then prints the message `` `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``, which only reports the relationship that was fitted and needs no action. Reference layers behave the same way: `geom_hline(yintercept = 0)` rules a horizontal line at zero, and section 5 uses one to split a figure into results that support a claim and results that do not.

Line thickness is set with `linewidth`, whereas point size and type size are set with `size`, and mixing the two up is behind a great many warnings.

```r
ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.4)   # the thickness of a drawn line
ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7)       # the area of a plotted point
ggplot2::geom_text(size = 3.5)        # the height of a piece of type
```

Passing `size` to a line geom still works, but R warns "Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. Please use `linewidth` instead." The reason that the two names survive side by side is that `size` on a point means an area and on text a height, neither of which is a line thickness.

### Scales

The mapping says which column drives colour; the **scale** decides which colours it drives, and the same holds for positions, sizes and shapes. Every mapping gets a default scale, and you override it whenever the default is not what a reader needs.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    name   = "Assistance programme",
    values = c("0" = "#848c94", "1" = "#a10000"),
    labels = c("0" = "none", "1" = "bailout")
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5))
```

`scale_colour_manual()` names a colour for each level of the variable. Giving `values` and `labels` as *named* vectors, with `"0" = …` rather than a bare pair, means the assignment cannot silently reverse itself if the data ever arrives in a different order. The colours that the course uses throughout are `#0e3b6a` (dark blue), `#E69F00` (orange), `#009E73` (green), `#a10000` (dark red) and `#848c94` (mid grey), with `#c7ccd2` reserved as the muted grey for results that are not statistically significant. The orange and green belong to a palette built to stay distinguishable under the commonest forms of colour vision deficiency, which is why the decks never rest an argument on a red-green contrast alone.

Position scales follow the same override logic, and one of their arguments catches people out. `scale_x_continuous(breaks = …)` decides where the tick marks fall, but the sibling argument `limits` **removes** every row outside the range before any statistic is computed, so a smoother is refitted on whatever rows remain.

```r
p_trend <- ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a")

p_trend + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.30, 0.50))   # drops rows, then refits
p_trend + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.30, 0.50))        # keeps every row, only zooms
```

Run the first of those and R warns "Removed 163 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`)", and the trend line you are looking at now runs through 107 country-years rather than 270. `coord_cartesian()` zooms the finished figure instead and leaves the computation untouched, so it is the one to use when you only want a closer look.

### Facets

**Faceting** repeats the same plot once per group, on shared axes, so the groups can be compared by eye instead of by disentangling overlapping series. A country-year table suits it well, since each country can have a panel of its own.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013))
```

Twenty-seven small panels appear, one per country code, each showing the cosmopolitan-framing series of that country across the decade. The browser lab of the EU-frames case draws the same figure with tinyplot early in the exercise, so that the crisis years are in view before any model is fitted and it is plain how differently the countries move. The `~ cntry` is a one-sided formula, with nothing to the left of the `~`. A model formula, as in `lm()`, uses the same syntax with an outcome written on the left. `ncol` fixes the shape of the grid. Where two grouping variables matter, `facet_grid(rows = vars(a), cols = vars(b))` crosses them into a matrix of panels.

### Labels and themes

Two layers finish a figure. `labs()` supplies the words – axis titles, plot title, subtitle, caption, legend name – and it deserves more care than beginners give it, because a column name such as `mcosmo` means nothing to a reader who has not opened the codebook. The **theme** then governs everything with no data behind it: type size, gridlines, background, the position of the legend.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x       = "Unemployment rate (%)",
    y       = "Cosmopolitan framing (mean score, 0–1)",
    title   = "Unemployment and cosmopolitan framing",
    caption = "270 country-years, EU-frames dataset"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    plot.title       = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position  = "top"
  )
```

`theme_minimal()` is the default look across the course, and `base_size` is its most useful argument, scaling every piece of type at once: 9 for a dense panel of small multiples, 12 for a page figure, 15 and upwards for a slide. A bare `theme()` afterwards overrides individual pieces, and the order matters, because a complete theme applied *after* your adjustments would wipe them out. Inside it, `element_blank()` deletes a piece outright, `element_text()` restyles type, and `element_line()` restyles rules and gridlines.

A plot is an ordinary R object, so you can store it under a name, extend it later, and write it to a file:

```r
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = "Cosmopolitan framing")

p + ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplot2::ggsave("figures/framing_unemployment.png", p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

`ggsave()` takes its dimensions in inches and writes whichever format the file extension names. When you do not name a plot, it saves the last one drawn, which is convenient but can save the wrong figure, so name the object.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Draw the scatterplot of `unemp` against `mcosmo`, then change one thing at a time and watch what moves. Swap `geom_point()` for `geom_text(aes(label = cntry))` and each point becomes its country code; move `colour = factor(bailout)` from inside `aes()` to outside it and read the error it raises; drop the `factor()` and compare the two legends. Then add `facet_wrap(~ year)` and decide for yourself whether ten panels tell you more than one crowded cloud does.
:::

### From the pipe to the plot

Reshaping and drawing usually happen in one chain, with datawizard passing its result straight to ggplot2. The chain uses `|>` while it is still working on data and switches to `+` once `ggplot()` appears.

```r
euframes |>
  datawizard::data_filter(year >= 2009) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(mean_unemp = mean(unemp), by = "cntry") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = reorder(cntry, mean_unemp), y = mean_unemp)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean unemployment, 2009–2013 (%)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

`reorder()` sorts the country codes by the value being plotted rather than alphabetically, which turns a jumble of bars into a ranking you can read at a glance. `geom_col()` draws a bar whose height is the number stored in the data, which is what you want once `data_summary()` has already done the counting; its cousin `geom_bar()` counts the rows for you instead, and reaching for the wrong one of the two is a frequent small frustration.

Where two figures belong side by side, the **patchwork** package composes whole plots. `patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)` sets two plot objects in a row, and `patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, nrow = 1)` does the same for a list of them; with the package attached by `library(patchwork)`, `p1 + p2` does it with the same `+` that adds layers.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Build a chain that keeps the crisis years, groups by `year`, and reports the mean of `mcosmo` and the mean of `mneg` per year, then pipe it into a plot with two `geom_line()` layers in different colours. You will find yourself wanting a legend and not getting one, because both colours were set rather than mapped. The remedy is to reshape the data into long form, with one row per year and outcome, using `data_to_long()` from datawizard (or `pivot_longer()` from tidyr), and then to map `colour` to the column that names the outcome.
:::

## 5. Reading the specification curve {#sec-speccurve}

The central figure of the course is a **specification curve**, and you now have every part needed to build one yourself. A hypothesis about a dataset admits many defensible analyses, and if you fit all of them and line the results up in order, you can see the range of answers that the data supports instead of the single answer that one analyst happened to report.

`data/spec_curve.csv` holds that curve for the EU-frames case: `r nrow(eu_curve)` rows, one per specification that the course judges a justifiable way of answering the claim, each recording the decisions that distinguish it from its neighbours, the partial correlation that it produced, and its p-values under several kinds of inference. The column `sig` records whether its p-value under standard errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom lies below 0.05, the test that the course uses to class every point (the [statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-inference) explains it), and `is_reference` marks the reference specification of the course, the analysis that analyst C6HJR submitted to Multi100, which is one of the three analyses that the one-day courses on the EU-frames case let you choose to reproduce in Task 3. Reading the file needs one preparatory step, which the paragraph after the code explains.

```r
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(r_ca = dplyr::if_else(predictor == "growth", -r, r)) |>   # claim alignment
  datawizard::data_arrange("r_ca") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n())

reference <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
```

The claim under test is that poor economic performance depresses the positive framing of the EU. With unemployment as the predictor, a negative correlation supports it, because a rise in unemployment is a worsening of the economy. With GDP growth as the predictor, support means a *positive* correlation instead, because a fall in growth is the worsening, and plotting the raw numbers together would scatter agreeing results on opposite sides of zero. **Claim alignment** repairs that. Flip the sign wherever the predictor is growth, and afterwards a negative value means support for every row alike. `if_else()` performs the flip, and the `_ca` suffix is the naming habit of the course for any claim-aligned quantity. The file already carries the aligned value in a column of the same name, so the line rebuilds something that you can check against the stored column. Sorting by the aligned value and numbering the rows then gives each specification a rank, and that rank becomes the horizontal axis.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(curve, ggplot2::aes(x = rank, y = r_ca)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(shape = sig), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = reference, colour = "#8b1538", size = 3) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text",
    x = reference$rank, y = reference$r_ca - 0.08,
    label = "the reference specification\n(C6HJR, t = -3.804)",
    colour = "#8b1538", fontface = "bold", size = 3.2, hjust = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    name   = NULL,
    values = c("TRUE" = 1, "FALSE" = 4),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "CR2 p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "CR2 p ≥ 0.05")
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.65, 0.2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x     = "specification, ranked by claim-aligned partial correlation",
    y     = "claim-aligned partial correlation",
    title = "The curve of the claim"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Almost everything in that block has come up already: a reference line, a layer of small points whose shape is mapped to a logical column, a second point layer drawn from a *different* data frame, a manual scale, a zoom, labels and a theme. The manual scale sets the convention of the charts of the course, an open circle for a result below the 5% threshold and a cross for one above it, drawn at the same size and in translucent ink so that dense stretches of the curve stay readable and the class of a point is read from its shape rather than from a colour. `data = reference` inside the geom overrides the frame given to `ggplot()`, and that is how a single row gets picked out and emphasised. `annotate()` is the one function you have not met. It adds a mark that comes from no column at all, since you supply the coordinates and the text yourself, and that is why its position is read off `reference` rather than mapped.

Every point below the grey line is an analysis in the direction of the claim. Of the `r nrow(eu_curve)` specifications, `r pct(100 * mean(eu_curve$supports))` lie below it and `r pct(100 * mean(eu_curve$supports & eu_curve$sig))` lie below it with a CR2 p-value under 0.05. The aligned correlations run from `r num(min(eu_curve$r_ca))` to `r num(max(eu_curve$r_ca))`, so the curve holds firm support and a few results on the other side of zero. The burgundy point is the reference specification, the analysis that C6HJR submitted to Multi100, with a t-statistic of −3.804. Of the other specifications, `r sum(eu_curve$r_ca < eu_ref$r_ca)` lie further below zero than it does, and with a CR2 p-value of `r num(eu_ref$p_cr2)` it is drawn as a cross. The submitted analysis was neither an outlier nor a cherry-pick, and yet the same menu, worked through in good faith by any competent analyst, would have produced a great many other numbers, most of them further in the direction of the claim.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Rebuild the curve, then add `colour = estimator` inside the `aes()` of the first point layer and delete the fixed `colour = "#0e3b6a"` that follows it, keeping the shapes as they are. The two colours largely separate along the ranking, which is why the estimator is the decision that moves the curve most, and the [Multiverse page](../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd) explains what the two designs compare. Then try `ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ predictor)` on the same figure and ask yourself which of the two pictures you would rather a reviewer saw.
:::

## Sources and further study {#sec-sources}

This module was written for the course and adapts no existing lesson, so there is no borrowed text to attribute. It teaches only the part of R that the materials of the course use, in the order in which the course needs it.

For a fuller, self-paced grounding in R, these open resources are recommended:

- **The Carpentries, "R for Reproducible Scientific Analysis" and "Programming with R".** <https://swcarpentry.github.io/r-novice-gapminder/> and <https://swcarpentry.github.io/r-novice-inflammation/>. Licensed CC BY 4.0, and the standard hands-on introductions to R for researchers, covering objects, vectors and data frames in far more depth than this page.
- **The Turing Way, "Guide for Reproducible Research".** <https://book.the-turing-way.org/>. Licensed CC BY 4.0. Not an R tutorial as such, but the best short statement of why the habits that this module practises – scripts over console history, relative paths, one file for analysis and report – are worth building from the first day.
- **"R for Data Science"**, the free book by the authors of the tidyverse packages, at <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/>. Its chapters on data transformation and on visualisation cover the dplyr counterparts of the datawizard verbs and the grammar of ggplot2 in full.
- **The documentation of the packages**, which is readable as an introduction as well as a reference: [easystats.github.io/datawizard](https://easystats.github.io/datawizard/), [grantmcdermott.com/tinyplot](https://grantmcdermott.com/tinyplot/), [dplyr.tidyverse.org](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/), [readr.tidyverse.org](https://readr.tidyverse.org/), [ggplot2.tidyverse.org](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/), [vincentarelbundock.github.io/tinytable](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/tinytable/), [easystats.github.io/easystats](https://easystats.github.io/easystats/), [haven.tidyverse.org](https://haven.tidyverse.org/), [readxl.tidyverse.org](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/), and the arrow R package site at [arrow.apache.org/docs/r](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/).

When you are ready for a first statistical model, the module on [the statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd) takes the linear model on to the panel models that the EU-frames case requires.
